elements.id-string-10: Most machine learning tasks amount to choosing an optimal Neural Network (NN).
elements.id-string-11: This  is usually done by first defining a loss function, which depends on various parameters of the NN (and number in millions in realistic applications), then one finds a suitable minima of the loss function, often by Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) \cite{EonBottou1998OnlineLA}.
elements.id-string-12: Thus gaining an understanding of the loss function landscape is crucial for machine learning.
elements.id-string-13: The loss function, also referred to as the cost function,  is in general a non-convex function.
elements.id-string-14: Finding a global minimum of a general non-convex function is hard \cite{10.1162/089976602760408035, livni2014computational, shalevshwartz2017failures}, in fact NP-hard \cite{Murty1987SomeNP}, \cite{10.5555/2969735.2969792}.
elements.id-string-15: Nevertheless in practice optimizing a Deep Neural Network (DNN) is usually possible.
elements.id-string-16: This has led many to believe that after all, for DNN-s the loss function does not have spurious local minima \cite{freeman2017topology, hoffer2018train, soudry2016bad}.
elements.id-string-17: This is indeed the case for shallow linear NN-s, which have only saddles and no local minima \cite{BALDI198953}.
elements.id-string-18: For  deep linear networks, all local minima of the  squared loss function are global, with other critical points being saddles \cite{kawaguchi2016deep}.
elements.id-string-19: It has been further argued  that the same holds true for non-linear networks, under certain assumptions \cite{kawaguchi2016deep}.
elements.id-string-20: For a fully connected network with squared loss and analytic activation function, all minima have been argued to be global \cite{nguyen2017loss}.
elements.id-string-21: Similar results were previously shown in \cite{107014, fra, 410380}.
elements.id-string-22: Although optimization of deep linear models exhibits some similarities with optimization of deep non-linear  models \cite{saxe2014exact},  ``local implies global'' picture seems not to carry over to non-linear DNN-s.
elements.id-string-23: e.g. spurious minima have been shown to exist for shallow Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) networks \cite{safran2018spurious}.
elements.id-string-24: It  has been suggested that absence of spurious local minima might be a feature specific to deep linear networks and might be destroyed as soon as non-linearity is introduced  \cite{yun2019small, zou2018stochastic, swirszcz2017local}.
elements.id-string-25: For Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) with  piecewise linear activation function, spurious minima have been argued to be common \cite{liu2021spurious}.
elements.id-string-26: Local or global, exponentially many minima seems to be a generic feature of the loss function.
elements.id-string-27: Typically DNNs involve millions of parameters, but even for moderately sized networks, the number of local optima and saddle points already shows exponential growth in the number of parameters \cite{NIPS1995_3806734b, NIPS1996_a51fb975, choromanska2015loss, pmlr-v38-choromanska15}.

elements.id-string-43: We point out that the physical potential of certain microscopic descriptions of black holes in string theory capture some key features of the loss landscape.
elements.id-string-44: The motivation for this work is to relate exponential degeneracy of loss function minima to the exponential degeneracy of quantum states in a statistical mechanical system.
elements.id-string-45: This connection can be made explicit for supersymmetric black holes, where the black hole entropy implies the existence of exponentially many degenerate states, which in turn can be related to the minima of a potential through supersymmetric quantum mechanics.

elements.id-string-47: A black hole carries an entropy $S_{BH} = \frac{A}{4 \ell_P^2}$, called Bekenstein-Hawking entropy \cite{Bekenstein1, Bekenstein2, BCH, Hawking75}.
elements.id-string-48: Here $A$ is the area of the event horizon of the black hole and $\ell_P= \sqrt{\frac{G \hbar}{c^3}}$ is the Planck length, G is the Newton's constant, $\hbar$ is the  Planck's constant and $c$ is velocity of light.
elements.id-string-49: Providing  a statistical mechanical interpretation of this entropy is a highly non-trivial challenge, supposed to be addressed by a theory of quantum gravity, such as string theory.
elements.id-string-50: In deed, $S_{BH}$ is reproduced from microscopic state counting in a wide variety of black holes in string theory \cite{Strominger:1996sh, Maldacena:1997de, Shih:2005qf}.
elements.id-string-51: It is done by providing a ``microscopic description'' of a black hole as a bound state of more fundamental solitonic objects in string theory, then coming up with a  low energy description  of that bound state dynamics and finally counting states carrying appropriate quantum numbers.

elements.id-string-77: A brief introduction to black hole entropy in string theory
elements.id-string-78: This section contains well known facts about black holes in string theory and readers familiar with the subject can skip this section.
elements.id-string-79: \paragraph{A quick introduction to black hole entropy:}
elements.id-string-80: Black holes are astronomical objects, formed by collapse of  dead stars.
elements.id-string-81: Their claim to fame is that nothing, not even light, can escape their gravitational  pull.
elements.id-string-82: From a theoretical perspective, black holes are solutions to Einstein's equations with event horizon.
elements.id-string-83: A curious feature of such solutions is that they are entirely fixed by a handful  of parameters, such as mass, angular  momentum, electric and magnetic charges etc, and therefore leaving no scope for any microstructure and hence any entropy.
elements.id-string-84: However this is rather problematic, since one could violate the second law of thermodynamics, by simply throwing an entropic object into a black hole.
elements.id-string-85: Making use of an existing result in classical gravity that area of the event horizon  of a black hole does not go down in a physical process \cite{PhysRevLett.26.1344}, Bekenstein proposed that a black hole should be assigned an entropy proportional to the area of its event horizon \cite{Bekenstein1, Bekenstein2}.
elements.id-string-86: In fact it was shown in \cite{BCH} that the ``laws of black hole mechanics'' have striking resemblance with the laws of black  hole mechanics, although it was unclear whether this was a coincidence or not.
elements.id-string-87: In particular a black hole with non-zero temperature, is expected to emit thermal radiation, which would contradict the very  definition of a black hole.
elements.id-string-88: This issue was settled by Hawking as he found that quantum mechanically black holes emit thermal radiation \cite{Hawking75}, with a temperature consistent with the findings of  \cite{BCH}.
elements.id-string-89: In particular, this work led to a precise formula for black hole entropy
elements.id-string-91: This remarkable finding however led to only deeper puzzles.
elements.id-string-92: Now that black holes are understood to have an entropy, as  per standard statistical mechanical understanding of entropy, there must also exist $e^{S_{BH}}$ black hole  microstates.
elements.id-string-93: Classical gravity leaves us clueless, whereas the appearance of the Planck length $\ell_P$ in the black hole entropy formula \refb{Sbh}, suggests that answers lie in a theory of quantum gravity, such as string theory.
elements.id-string-94: \paragraph{How black holes arise in string theory:}
elements.id-string-95: The low energy physics of string theory is captured by supergravity theories.
elements.id-string-96: These supergravity theories have black hole solutions.
elements.id-string-97: The black holes considered in this paper, are of this type.
elements.id-string-98: By  the virtue of being embedded in string theory, it is often possible have an understanding of their microstates.
elements.id-string-99: We will restrict to black hole solutions, that preserve some supersymmetry.
elements.id-string-100: Such black holes are extremal, namely ``their charge equals mass''.
elements.id-string-101: Here charge refers to charge (both electric and magnetic) under various U(1) gauge fields of supergravity.
elements.id-string-102: These charges are meaningful even beyond four dimensional supergravity, in particulars their carriers can be identified as membrane  like objects (called D-branes) in full string theory.
elements.id-string-103: This provides an alternative description of black holes as bound states of D-branes.
elements.id-string-104: This description, usually referred to as microscopic description, makes the microstates manifest.
elements.id-string-105: Extremal black holes carry zero temperature and hence the entropy is simply the logarithm of ground state degeneracy\footnote{The distinction between degeneracy and the index (the $14^{th}$ helicity supertrace in this case) is not too relevant for this work.}.
elements.id-string-106: The potential landscape in microscopic description of black holes
elements.id-string-107: In most well known examples, the microscopic description of black holes is a two dimensional  Conformal Field Theory (CFT) \cite{Strominger:1996sh, Maldacena:1997de}.
elements.id-string-108: In such description, one looks for degeneracy of states at a given CFT level, which is captured by Cardy formula \cite{PhysRevLett.26.1344}.
elements.id-string-109: In this approach there is no energy landscape involved.
elements.id-string-110: Since we are looking for a potential landscape with ground states corresponding to its minima, quantum mechanical, i.e. 0+1 dimensional microscopic descriptions are better suited.
elements.id-string-111: For supersymmetric black holes, this quantum mechanics is supersymmetric, i.e. preserves some supercharges, which annihilate the ground states.
elements.id-string-112: For supersymmetric  quantum mechanics (SQM), it is known that the index $\mathcal{I} := N_B - N_F$ is  given by the Euler characteristic of the vacuum manifold, i.e. manifold on which the potential vanishes \cite{Witten_morse, Schellekens_Warner, Witten_elliptic}.
elements.id-string-113: Since the potential is a sum of squares in this case, vacuum manifold is also the space of minima.
